people.name: Dolores "Lola" Reyes
people.situation: Quezon City, Philippines. Retired public elementary school teacher, widowed six years. Lives in the family house with her unmarried son (41) and half-raises a niece's two small children. Small pension; runs a sari-sari store from the front window. Parish choir and Legion of Mary. High blood pressure and bad knees.
people.temperament: She is awake at 4:30, sweeping the front step and humming before the rooster next door has finished. By seven she has sent "Good morning, God bless!" with a sunflower picture to three family group chats. She talks to everyone: the tricycle driver, the girl at the pharmacy, the new priest whose homilies she thinks are too short. She remembers birthdays, sends pancit to the wake of a man she met twice, and lends money to nephews who never quite pay it back. When someone thanks her she waves it away, but she notices who doesn't, and a small list of those people lives in her head for years. She cannot stand a quiet room and fills it with stories, some of them told before. When she is hurt she does not shout. She goes quiet, serves food with great politeness, and says "It's okay, anak" in a voice that makes it clear it is not. At night she worries about money and about her son, who has no wife and no steady work, but in the morning she decides not to think about it and makes coffee. She laughs easily, cries at soap operas, and is proud of her old pupils who became nurses abroad. She can be bossy about how rice should be cooked and how a table should be set. She prays the rosary on the jeepney, lips moving, while listening closely to the conversation behind her.
people.friend_view: Tessie from the choir says Lola would give you her last peso and then mention it to you, kindly, for the next ten years. She needs to be needed and gets restless when nobody asks her for anything. She spoils her son and complains about him to everyone except him. She never lets anyone look after her: when she was in hospital she ended up organising the ward.
people.self_view: A simple, happy person who likes helping. Not very clever, just blessed. She would say she forgives easily and never keeps score.
people.faith: Devout Catholic. Daily rosary, Sunday Mass, First Fridays, a Santo Nino on the shelf. Her faith is warm and practical, full of saints and novenas; she rarely thinks about doctrine.
people.weighing: Whether to ask her nephew for the 30,000 pesos he borrowed for a motorbike, because she now needs it for her own blood-pressure medicine and a knee injection. Underneath that, whether her son will be all right when she is gone.

people.name: Marcus Webb
people.situation: Leeds, England. Night-shift supervisor at a parcel warehouse. Divorced two years; has his daughter Ellie (8) every other weekend. Rents a flat above a vape shop. Money is tight after child maintenance. Drinking more than he used to.
people.temperament: Marcus is quick. Quick to laugh, quick to help lift something, quick to lose it. On shift he knows every lad's name and whose mum is poorly, and he'll cover a break without being asked. But if a scanner fails for the third time or someone answers back, his face goes red and he's shouting before he knows he's started, and the whole bay goes quiet. Ten minutes later he's buying the lad a can from the machine and saying "no hard feelings, yeah?" as if that settles it. He hates waiting: queues, phone menus, his ex's solicitor. In traffic he swears at other drivers, then feels a hot flash of shame when he catches Ellie's eyes in the mirror. After nights he can't sleep, so he has four or five cans and watches football highlights until noon. He tells himself it's to wind down. He's funny, does voices, and is brilliant with kids in short bursts. He struggles to say sorry properly, in words; he'd rather fix your car. When he's low he goes silent for days and ignores messages, then turns up with a takeaway as if nothing happened. He is loyal to a fault and would square up to anyone who disrespected his mates. He keeps Ellie's drawings on the fridge and a photo of his nan in his wallet.
people.friend_view: His mate Dean says Marcus has the biggest heart and the shortest fuse he has ever seen, and he has no idea how frightening he is when he goes off. People walk on eggshells round him, Ellie included. The drinking is worse than he admits, and he blames his ex for everything.
people.self_view: Honest and straightforward: he says what everyone else is thinking, it's over in a minute, and he never holds a grudge. A good dad who got a raw deal. He does not think he has a drinking problem, just a rough patch.
people.faith: Christened Church of England and went to a church primary school. Hasn't been inside a church except for weddings and his nan's funeral. Unsure; says "there's probably something" and prays now and then when he's frightened.
people.weighing: Last weekend Ellie asked him why he shouts so much. He has thought about it more than he'd admit. He is also wondering whether to take a day-shift job that pays less so he can see her more.

people.name: Tomasz Nowak
people.situation: Krakow, Poland. Structural engineer who checks bridge and road designs. Married 27 years to Beata; three children aged 26, 23 and 17. Their flat in Nowa Huta is paid off and they have a small allotment. Comfortable but careful. Some back trouble.
people.temperament: Tomasz does not rush. Asked a question at dinner, he chews, thinks, and answers half a minute later, by which time his wife has usually answered for him. At work he is the one who rechecks the calculations everyone else has signed off, and he is usually right, which makes him quietly unpopular with younger colleagues. He writes every expense in a notebook, drives a fourteen-year-old Skoda he services himself, and cannot understand why his children pay for three streaming services. He puts off decisions for months: the bathroom renovation has been "next spring" for six springs. But once he starts something he finishes it properly, and the shed he built on the allotment has not leaked in eleven years. He dislikes arguments and leaves the room rather than raise his voice, but he does not change his mind. He simply goes on doing it his way. He is uneasy with feelings and shows love by fixing things, driving people to the airport at four in the morning, and slipping his daughter money she doesn't know came from him. He likes long walks in the Tatras, alone or with one person who doesn't need to talk. He reads military history. Small talk tires him, and at family name-day parties he stands by the window with a plate he never finishes.
people.friend_view: Beata says he is as reliable as a wall and just as hard to move. Generous in secret and stingy in public: she has to fight him for every zloty spent on anything enjoyable. He is kinder than he lets anyone see.
people.self_view: A practical, sensible man who doesn't waste things, words included. He believes he is open to other views; he simply finds most of them wrong.
people.faith: Catholic. Mass every Sunday without fail, confession before Easter, never joins the hymns. His belief is solid and unexamined. He dislikes priests who talk politics from the pulpit.
people.weighing: His youngest wants to study in the Netherlands, which would use money he has saved for emergencies. His father is getting forgetful, and his brother assumes Tomasz will handle it.

people.name: Adaeze Okafor
people.situation: Lagos, Nigeria. Product manager at a fintech company; unmarried; shares a flat in Yaba. Earns well by local standards and sends money to her parents in Enugu and for her younger brother's school fees. Her mother asks every week when she will marry.
people.temperament: Adaeze has four notebooks, each for a different venture: a skincare line, a tutoring app, a podcast about women in tech, and an event-rental company that already owns forty plastic chairs. The chairs are in her mum's garage. She works twelve-hour days and then does "just one more thing" at midnight. She cannot watch a film without her phone, taps her foot in meetings, and plans her week in colour-coded blocks that she abandons by Wednesday. In a room she is brilliant: fast, funny, convincing, and people agree to things they never meant to. She is first to volunteer and first to lose interest once the novelty wears off; the dull middle of a project makes her feel almost physically itchy. She is warm to strangers, mentors secondary-school girls for free, and will send fifty thousand naira to a stranger's hospital bill from a WhatsApp broadcast without checking. With people who are slow she is sharp and sighs out loud. On the rare evenings she is alone, because she fills them, she sometimes feels a sudden flat dread she can't name, and she gets up and cleans. She hates being told what to do, most of all by her mother. On Sundays she loves the music at church and hates the length.
people.friend_view: Her friend Chioma says Ada starts things the way other people breathe and finishes almost nothing, leaving a trail of half-built projects and slightly let-down partners. She is so busy helping everybody that nobody can get close to her. She can't rest, and it isn't only ambition: she is scared of stillness.
people.self_view: A builder and a visionary who makes things happen while others only talk. She thinks her problem is too little time, not too many projects.
people.faith: Pentecostal evangelical. Attends a large Lagos church, tithes, speaks often of God's plan for her life. Prays in bursts, often while stuck in traffic; reads a daily devotional app about half the days.
people.weighing: A co-founder wants her to quit her job and go full time on the tutoring app. Her mother is setting her up with a church elder's son. She has also noticed she hasn't slept more than five hours a night in a month.

people.name: Eleni Papadaki
people.situation: A village outside Chania, Crete. Widowed eleven years; her son Giorgos died of a heart attack at 43 two years ago. Lives alone in the old house with olive trees and a few hens. Her daughter-in-law Maria and two grandchildren live in Chania town. Small pension. Heart medication and failing eyesight.
people.temperament: Eleni still wears black and will for the rest of her life, and she sees nothing strange in that. She rises early, feeds the hens, lights the oil lamp before the icons, and then sits in the doorway with her hands in her lap for a long time. She speaks little, and when she does it is to the point and often cutting. She tells her daughter-in-law the children are too thin and the lentils too salty. She keeps count of who came to Giorgos's memorials and who didn't. She walks to the cemetery every day, even in the August heat, to tend his grave and fill the little lamp, and she talks to him there more than to anyone living. Neighbours bring her things and she accepts them with little thanks, then sends back twice as much in eggs and oil. She is hard to comfort and distrusts people who try; she thinks cheerful people simply haven't lived yet. She can be funny in a dry, bleak way that surprises visitors. She is stubborn about doctors, about modern kitchens, about phones at her table. At night she cannot sleep and sits in the dark with her prayer rope, not always saying the prayer, sometimes just holding it.
people.friend_view: Her sister Katerina says Eleni was always proud and hard, and after Giorgos died she closed like a fist. She is cruel to Maria without meaning to be, because Maria is alive and her son isn't. She won't let anyone help her, and she is terribly lonely.
people.self_view: A plain woman who has had a hard life and knows her duty. She doesn't think she is harsh, only honest, and she thinks young people are soft.
people.faith: Greek Orthodox. Liturgy on Sundays, strict fasting, icons in every room, the memorial services at forty days, one year and now two. Faith is part of her body. She is angry with God and would never say it aloud.
people.weighing: Maria has asked her to come and live with them in Chania. Eleni doesn't want to leave the grave or the house, and doesn't want to be a burden. The doctor says she should not be living alone.

people.name: Jake Sorensen
people.situation: St. Cloud, Minnesota, USA. First year at a community college, no major chosen. Works 25 hours a week at a hardware store and lives with his mom and stepdad. Plays video games most nights until three or four. Already $4,000 in student loans.
people.temperament: Jake is easy to be around. He laughs at your jokes, agrees with your opinions, and remembers your dog's name. With his gym friends he talks about lifting and crypto; with his friend from English class he talks about climate and therapy; with his stepdad he talks about the Vikings. In each place he means it at the time. His opinion of a movie depends on who he watched it with. Customers at the store like him because he's patient with old men hunting for the right bolt, but he is always a few minutes late. He starts things with real enthusiasm, a YouTube channel, a morning running routine, a Bible reading plan his grandma mailed him, and they last about nine days. Nights disappear into games and short videos, and he tells himself that tomorrow he'll go to bed at a normal time. Under the jokes he is anxious about almost everything ahead of him: picking a major, money, whether he's already behind everyone else. He hates conflict so much he'll text "haha yeah" to something he completely disagrees with. He is sweet with his little half-sister and picks her up from school without complaining. He rarely says what he actually wants, partly because he isn't sure.
people.friend_view: His friend Kayla says Jake is the nicest guy she knows and has no spine at all: he agrees with whoever talked to him last, and she's never sure what he really thinks. He is far more stressed than he acts, and he games so he doesn't have to think.
people.self_view: Chill, open-minded, easygoing, gets along with everybody, doesn't take things too seriously. He figures it will all work itself out.
people.faith: Raised Lutheran (ELCA), confirmed at 14, stopped going at 16. Unsure. He watches apologetics clips and atheist clips back to back and finds both convincing.
people.weighing: His advisor says he must choose a program by spring. A friend is pushing him toward an electrician apprenticeship; his mom wants him to transfer to the state university. He hasn't told either of them what he thinks.

people.name: Grace Mwangi
people.situation: Nairobi, Kenya. Senior nurse on a maternity ward at a county hospital. Married to Peter, a secondary school teacher; four children aged 9 to 19. Also supports her widowed mother in Nyeri. School fees stretch everything. Long shifts and a bad back.
people.temperament: On the ward Grace is calm, warm and unhurried. A frightened teenage mother at three in the morning gets her hand held and a joke. Junior nurses fear and adore her: she corrects them sharply and then quietly covers their mistakes. She can run a ward with half the staff it needs and never look rattled. At home it is different. She walks in tired, sees shoes in the corridor and a pot left unwashed, and her voice changes. She gives orders, sighs heavily, and tells Peter what he should have done. The children tiptoe until she has eaten. She knows this, and it bothers her at night, but by the next evening it happens again. She trusts her own judgement, decides fast, and does not like being second-guessed, least of all by her husband. At home she keeps money tight because the fees frighten her, yet she gives freely to colleagues' funeral collections and fundraisers. She sleeps five hours, squeezes in her savings-group meeting on Saturdays, and dozes off during the sermon. On the phone with her sisters she laughs until she has to sit down. She is proud of her work, and she rarely says she is tired.
people.friend_view: Her sister Wanjiru says Grace is a saint to strangers and a sergeant to her own family: the patients get her patience and the children get whatever is left. She believes she has to carry everything herself and won't let Peter carry anything.
people.self_view: A responsible, strong woman who keeps things together; firm at home because someone has to be. She thinks she is fair to everyone.
people.faith: Anglican Church of Kenya; a Mothers' Union member who attends when her shifts allow. Her faith is steady and practical. She prays a short prayer before every delivery.
people.weighing: Her 19-year-old daughter wants to leave her nursing course and study music, and Grace reacted badly. She is also deciding whether to take a better-paid job at a private hospital that would mean even longer hours.

people.name: Daniel Kim (Kim Do-hyun)
people.situation: Bundang, near Seoul, South Korea. Mid-level manager at a large electronics company. Married to Soo-jin; one son, Min-jun (10), who attends several evening academies. Big mortgage on their apartment. Commutes eighty minutes each way. Insomnia and acid reflux.
people.temperament: Daniel checks things. He checks the gas before leaving, checks his son's homework after the tutor has already checked it, checks his work email at red lights and in the church car park. He rarely feels finished with anything. At work he is dependable, polite to his superiors and quietly demanding of his team; he rewrites their reports late at night rather than send them back. At home he is there and not there: phone in hand, half-listening, then suddenly stern about a maths score. He worries in loops about the mortgage, his parents' health, whether his son will get into a good middle school, whether he'll be passed over for promotion. He cannot nap. On holiday he spends the first three days tense and the last day dreading the return. He rarely gets loud when he is angry; he goes cold and precise, which his wife finds worse. He is generous with his parents and pays for things before anyone asks. He is good at golf and quietly fierce about winning. Every so often, late at night, he watches old variety shows and laughs alone in the dark living room, and for twenty minutes he feels like himself.
people.friend_view: Soo-jin says he calls it responsibility but it is control: he doesn't trust anyone to do anything right, including her. Min-jun is starting to be afraid of disappointing him. He is a kind man who is never really in the room.
people.self_view: A responsible husband and father doing what is needed for his family's future. He believes he is the one keeping everything from falling apart, and that his worrying is just good sense.
people.faith: Presbyterian, in a large evangelical Korean church. Sunday worship, a weekly cell group, serves as a deacon. He believes firmly, but his prayers often turn into a list of worries.
people.weighing: Soo-jin wants to drop two of Min-jun's academies and Daniel is afraid he will fall behind. His company has offered him a two-year posting in Vietnam.

people.name: Maria Fernanda Silva
people.situation: Sao Paulo, Brazil (East Zone). Owns a small two-chair hair salon. Raising her son Rafael (7) alone; his father is not involved. About R$18,000 in credit-card and overdraft debt from fitting out the salon and a Christmas she couldn't afford. Lives near her mother, who helps with Rafael.
people.temperament: Maria Fernanda fills a room. She plays pagode loud in the salon, knows every client's love life, and says exactly what she thinks of their ex-husbands. She laughs with her whole body and hugs people she met an hour ago. She is quick with her tongue too: if a client is rude or a supplier overcharges, she flares up, says something she can't take back, and then stews over it for a day. She buys things when she is happy and when she is sad: a new dryer, sneakers for Rafael, a dinner for her girlfriends that she pays for "because I owe them." She hides the card statements in a kitchen drawer. She is endlessly generous with her time. She did a neighbour's daughter's hair for her fifteenth-birthday party for free, and she sits with her mother at the clinic for hours without complaint. She starts a diet every Monday. She is brave in obvious ways, walking alone at night to fetch her son, and scared in quiet ones, like opening the bank app. When Rafael is asleep she sometimes sits on the back step and cries for ten minutes, then scrolls on her phone, then goes to bed. She loves quickly and trusts too fast.
people.friend_view: Her friend Jaqueline says Fe is the most loving person she knows and a disaster with money: she spends to feel better and to be liked. Her temper has driven off good clients. She needs someone to sit her down and make her look at the numbers.
people.self_view: A fighter who does everything alone and still keeps smiling. She thinks her money troubles are bad luck and a slow economy.
people.faith: Baptised and raised Catholic; stopped going as a teenager. For three months she has gone with a client to an evangelical church. She loves the worship and the people but feels judged about Rafael's father. A seeker.
people.weighing: The pastor's wife has offered to help her make a budget and she is embarrassed to say yes. A man from the church has also started messaging her.

people.name: Bob Haskins
people.situation: Chillicothe, Ohio, USA. Retired machinist, 42 years at a paper mill. Married 54 years to June, who was diagnosed with Alzheimer's eighteen months ago. Two grown children in other states. Owns his house outright. Bad knee; a hearing aid he doesn't wear.
people.temperament: Bob is an ordinary, steady man. He gets up at six, makes June's oatmeal the way she likes it, and does the crossword in pen, not very well. He is patient most of the time, but sometimes, after June asks the same question for the fifth time in an hour, he goes out to the garage and bangs around for a while, then comes back in and answers her again gently. He is no talker. At the diner with the retired guys on Tuesdays he mostly listens and then adds one dry line that makes them all laugh. He'll help anyone move a couch but won't ask for help himself. He is careful with money without being cheap: he tips the waitress well and buys cookies from every Girl Scout who knocks. He can be stubborn about small things. He won't see a doctor about the knee, won't learn video calls, and won't let his daughter hire a home aide yet. In the evenings he gets a little blue and watches old westerns. He is mostly content, a bit worried, a bit lonely, and doesn't think too hard about any of it. He mows the widow next door's lawn without being asked. He still holds June's hand in church.
people.friend_view: His son Mike says Dad is the most decent man he knows and too proud to admit he is drowning looking after Mom. He isn't falling apart; he's just wearing out.
people.self_view: A regular guy doing what anybody would. He doesn't need a fuss made.
people.faith: United Methodist; the same congregation he joined in 1971, where he ushers at the early service. His faith is quiet and settled. He would rather do something for someone than talk about God.
people.weighing: His daughter wants to hire a part-time aide and start looking at memory-care homes. He doesn't want strangers in the house. His knee is getting worse.

people.name: Siobhan Gallagher
people.situation: Galway, Ireland. Secondary school English teacher. Married to Colm, a physiotherapist; two teenagers aged 15 and 13. A mortgage, comfortable enough. Her mother lives nearby and is getting frail.
people.temperament: Siobhan is funny in a sharp, sideways way. She has a remark for everything: the principal's new initiative, the weather, the parish newsletter. Her pupils love her because she is merciless and fair; she tears a lazy essay apart and then lends the kid a book she thinks will change their life. She reads the news too much and argues online at eleven at night with strangers about housing and the Church, then lies awake replaying it. She expects the worst, says so out loud, and is quietly delighted when she is wrong. She can't abide sentimentality in public and cries alone at films, at ads, at her son's terrible drawings from when he was six, which she keeps in a folder. She is loyal but easily hurt, and when she is hurt she gets cutting rather than sad. She has two glasses of wine most nights and sometimes three. She walks the prom at Salthill every morning in all weathers. With her mother she is impatient on the phone, then drives over with the shopping and stays three hours. At dinner parties she talks a great deal and says almost nothing about herself.
people.friend_view: Her friend Aoife says Siobhan thinks she is a hard-headed realist, but she's the softest person in any room. The cynicism is armour and it's getting thicker. She is more hurt by the Church than angry with it, and more tired than she lets on.
people.self_view: The realist, the one who sees through things. Not easily fooled, not sentimental.
people.faith: Raised Catholic, convent school. Stopped going in her twenties after the abuse reports. Still goes at Christmas and for funerals, and catches herself saying the old prayers when frightened. Calls herself "culturally Catholic, spiritually undecided."
people.weighing: Her mother wants a priest to anoint her and wants Siobhan there. Her daughter has asked to be confirmed "for the party." She doesn't know what to say to either of them.

people.name: Samuel Tesfaye
people.situation: Silver Spring, Maryland, USA. Came from Addis Ababa four years ago. Drives rideshare fifty hours a week and studies accounting at a community college at night. Shares a two-bedroom apartment with three other Ethiopian men. Sends $600 a month home to his mother and sisters.
people.temperament: Samuel is quiet and orderly. His car is spotless, with a small cross and a card of St. Gabriel on the dashboard. Passengers talk at him and he listens well, asks one small question, remembers details; many tip more than they meant to. He rarely speaks about himself. He eats cheaply, cooking injera and lentils on Sunday for the whole week, owns two pairs of shoes, and tracks every dollar in a spreadsheet. Other drivers call him stubborn because he won't cut corners or chase the late-night bar crowds he finds degrading. He is slow to trust and slow to decide, but once he decides he doesn't waver. He fasts on Wednesdays and Fridays and through the long fasts, even on twelve-hour driving days. On a rare free evening he walks alone on the creek trail with church songs in his headphones. He is lonely in a way he has no English words for. His roommates' noise and mess irritate him, but he says nothing, and the irritation piles up until he goes to stay at a cousin's for a weekend. On video calls with his little sisters he laughs a lot and teases them. He feels guilty whenever he buys anything for himself.
people.friend_view: His cousin Yonas says Samuel is the most reliable man he knows and is wearing himself thin for everyone back home. He never lets himself enjoy anything. He needs a wife, or at least one real friend here.
people.self_view: A son with duties. He doesn't think he is lonely, just busy. He believes he is more patient than he actually is.
people.faith: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo. Attends a parish in the DC area when he can, stands through the long services, keeps the fasts. His faith is deep and not bookish.
people.weighing: His mother is pressing him to come home and marry. A young woman at church has been kind to him and he doesn't know how to begin. He also failed one accounting exam and has to retake it.

people.name: Chloe Barrett
people.situation: Brisbane, Australia. Final-year nursing student; works as a barista 20 or more hours a week. Lives in a share house with four others. Her parents are divorced and she is the go-between. Student loan, no savings.
people.temperament: Chloe says sorry about forty times a day, including to furniture. She takes the extra shift whenever her manager asks, even on her exam weekend. She lets housemates eat her food and leave their dishes, and then she washes them, fuming silently, and feels guilty for fuming. She rewrites a text five times before sending it. On placement she is gentle with patients and good at noticing when someone is scared; she is less good at telling a doctor he has got something wrong. She overthinks everything: whether she offended someone, whether a chest twinge is nerves or her heart, whether her friends actually like her. Once she relaxes she is funny, with a goofy, self-mocking humour, and she is a good listener; people tell her things they tell no one else. She can't make small decisions, like what to order, and says "whatever you're having." When she's stressed she runs along the river, and it helps. Six months ago a friend from uni was killed in a car crash, and now Chloe reads the Gospel of Luke on her phone in bed at night and tells nobody. She is never sure whether what she feels when she reads it is real or whether she is making it up.
people.friend_view: Her housemate Priyanka says Chloe is a doormat, a lovely one: everyone takes advantage, she lets them, and then she worries she's being selfish for minding. She is much stronger than she thinks.
people.self_view: A bit of a mess, too anxious, not very interesting, but trying hard. She thinks she is selfish far more often than she is.
people.faith: Grew up with no religion. A seeker: after the funeral she started reading the Gospels, and she has been alone to one big contemporary service and one quiet Anglican evening service. She liked the quieter one.
people.weighing: Whether to go back to the Anglican church, and whether to tell anyone she has been. Both her mum and her dad want her for Christmas, and she is afraid of choosing.

people.name: Viktor Petrenko
people.situation: Wroclaw, Poland, from Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine. Was a mechanic at a bus depot; fled with his wife Halyna in 2022 when shelling reached their district. Now works at a car repair shop for less than his Polish colleagues. His son Andriy (32) is serving in the Ukrainian army; a daughter lives in Krakow. Back pain. Stopped heavy drinking two years ago.
people.temperament: Viktor wakes before the alarm and checks his phone for a message from Andriy before anything else. If there is one, even just a thumbs-up, the day is possible. If there isn't, he is gruff and silent until evening. He is a good mechanic and knows it; he can hear a bearing going from across the shop, and the Polish owner has started asking his opinion. He speaks little Polish and doesn't try hard to learn more, which frustrates his wife. At breaks he smokes on the back step and watches the street. He never complains about his own pain but complains a great deal about politicians, prices, the weather and young people. He expects bad news and braces for it. He has a heavy, unexpected kindness: he fixed a neighbour's elderly mother's car for nothing and refused money three times. He quit drinking when his hands began to shake, did it alone, and told nobody. He is stubborn: once he decides a person isn't serious, nothing will change his view. Some days he sits in the car after work for half an hour before going up to the flat. He rarely laughs, but when he does it is a real laugh, usually at something absurd on the television.
people.friend_view: Halyna says he has always been a closed door, and the war bolted it. He carries everything and tells nobody. He is kinder than his face.
people.self_view: A practical man with no complaints who does what needs doing. He doesn't think of himself as gloomy, only realistic.
people.faith: Grew up with little religion under the Soviets, though his grandmother had him baptised Orthodox. After the invasion he began going with Halyna to a Ukrainian Orthodox parish in Wroclaw and lights a candle for Andriy every Sunday. He doesn't know what he believes, but he goes.
people.weighing: Andriy's unit has been moved closer to the front. Halyna wants to talk about whether to go home when the war ends or stay in Poland, and he can't bring himself to think about it. The owner has offered him a proper contract.

people.name: Priya Thomas
people.situation: Bengaluru, India, originally from Kottayam, Kerala. Test lead at a mid-sized software company. Married to Joel, a bank officer; two children aged 8 and 4. Rents a flat in Whitefield. Her parents in Kerala are getting older. Mild thyroid condition.
people.temperament: Priya is ordinary, knows it, and doesn't mind. Mornings are a scramble: tiffin boxes, the school van, the four-year-old's missing shoe. She is calm most days and snappy on some, usually Mondays or after a bad night. At work she is competent and dependable and not loudly ambitious; she will speak up in a meeting if something is wrong, but she won't fight about it twice. She enjoys a gossip over filter coffee with a friend from the next team. She calls her mother most evenings and sometimes finds the calls long. She is reasonably careful with money: saves a little each month, splurges on a sari at Onam, feels a bit guilty, and gets over it. She likes company, and she also likes the hour after the children sleep when she watches a Malayalam film alone on the sofa. She loses her temper with Joel over the dishes about once a week, and they make up by morning. Every January she starts a walking routine and keeps it for about half the year. She is neither a worrier nor carefree. She worries about her parents' health and her son's reading, then gets busy and forgets for a while. She is kind without making a show of it.
people.friend_view: Her friend Anu says Priya is the most sensible one in their group and easy to be with. Maybe a little too quick to go along with her in-laws' plans to keep the peace. Solid.
people.self_view: A normal working mother doing her best. Nothing special, and fine with that.
people.faith: Mar Thoma Syrian Church, a Reformed church rooted in Kerala. Sunday worship in Malayalam, Sunday school for the children, family prayer most nights, though it gets skipped. She believes simply and doesn't dwell on it.
people.weighing: Whether to move back to Kerala in a few years to be near her parents, which would mean Joel changing jobs. Also whether to accept a promotion that means late-night calls with the US team.

people.name: Luis Hernandez
people.situation: Guadalajara, Mexico. Started a taco stand at 22; now owns a small birria-and-tortas restaurant with nine employees and has just bought a second location. Married to Rocio; five children aged 8 to 24. Type 2 diabetes diagnosed three years ago.
people.temperament: Luis is loud, warm and always moving. He greets regulars by name, hugs the delivery men, jokes with the priest who eats free on Thursdays, and quietly pays for a stranger's lunch when he sees the man counting coins. He cannot sit through a whole meal; he is up checking the kitchen, the till, the salsa. He starts every day at five and falls asleep in front of the football at ten. With his staff he is generous at Christmas and hot-headed on a busy Saturday: if an order comes out wrong he shouts, bangs a pot, and ten minutes later brings the cook a cold Coke by way of apology. He eats constantly, tasting everything, and ignores his glucose readings. His wife hides the sweet bread and he always finds it. He is stubborn about the diabetes, jokes about it, and gets irritable if anyone brings it up. With his children he is affectionate but mostly absent, because he is at the restaurant. He cries at his mother's grave and at his daughter's graduation. He has never read a contract all the way through. He trusts people, sometimes the wrong ones. He loves a big party and always pays for too much of it.
people.friend_view: His compadre Arturo says Luis would give you the shirt off his back and then yell at you for wrinkling it. He is working himself to death and eating himself to death and laughing it off. His kids miss him.
people.self_view: A hard worker who came from nothing, a good provider, a lucky man God has blessed. He thinks his temper is just how men in his family are and that the doctor exaggerates.
people.faith: Catholic. Devoted to Our Lady of Guadalupe, whose picture hangs by the register. Goes to Mass most Sundays, usually late, and walks the October pilgrimage to Zapopan. His faith is heartfelt and a little like a deal: he makes promises in return for favours.
people.weighing: His doctor has mentioned insulin and possible nerve damage in his feet. His eldest son wants to run the second location with new ideas Luis doesn't trust.

people.name: Hannah Brandt
people.situation: Hamburg, Germany. Retired early from a university library. Never married, no children. Lives alone in a rented flat in Eimsbuettel with a cat named Fontane. Comfortable pension, spent carefully. An older sister in Bremen; they speak monthly. Hip pain.
people.temperament: Hannah's days are orderly and she likes them that way: coffee at seven, the newspaper crossword, a walk along the Alster, library books in strict rotation, a list on the fridge. She finds most people slightly too loud and too eager, and she is relieved when visits end. She notices small things: a misused word, a dripping tap, a neighbour's recycling in the wrong bin, which she reports to the building manager. She is precise with money and has an opinion about what everything ought to cost. She is kind in quiet, unannounced ways, feeding a neighbour's cat, bringing soup to the old man downstairs, and she would be embarrassed to be thanked. She is sharply critical of her sister's choices, her sister's husband, and the names of her sister's grandchildren. She reads Fontane, Rilke and Scandinavian detective novels. Sundays sometimes stretch long and silent, and she tells herself this is peace. When a friend from her old job died last year, she found she had no one to tell. She is slow to begin anything new: she turned down a reading circle twice before going. Now she goes, says little, and looks forward to it all month.
people.friend_view: Her old colleague Ingrid says Hannah insists she is perfectly content alone, but she is lonelier than she knows, and her sharpness keeps people at arm's length before they can let her down. She is more generous than anyone sees and harsher about her sister than is fair.
people.self_view: Self-sufficient, content and sensible. She has chosen a quiet life and needs very little. She believes she is tolerant.
people.faith: Baptised and confirmed Lutheran; still pays church tax. Goes to the Christmas Eve service at St. Michael's and to concerts in churches. Unsure. She is moved more by Bach cantatas than by sermons and sometimes wonders whether that counts.
people.weighing: Her hip operation is booked and she will need help for six weeks. Her sister has offered to come and stay. Hannah dreads it.

people.name: Andre Jackson
people.situation: Atlanta, Georgia, USA. Associate youth pastor at a mid-sized Baptist church; studying part-time at an online seminary. Engaged to Brianna, wedding in May. Modest salary. About $9,000 in debt from sports-betting apps, which nobody knows about.
people.temperament: Andre lights up a room and knows it. On Wednesday nights he preaches to eighty teenagers in sneakers and a hoodie, drops references from their feeds, gets them laughing and then gets them quiet. Kids text him at midnight and he answers. He is quick, confident, great on a microphone, and he hates a pause in a conversation. He is generous with his time and remembers every kid's name and their little brother's. He is also restless: he can't sit through a staff meeting without checking his phone, and what he's often checking is a bet on the Hawks. It began as fun with friends two years ago. Now he chases losses, tells himself the next one will clear it, and has a second credit card Brianna has never seen. When he loses big he is extra cheerful at church. He is quick to counsel others and slow to take counsel. With his senior pastor he is deferential; with volunteers he can be curt when things aren't done his way. In private he is very hard on himself and rarely lets anyone see it. He calls his mother every day. He prays honestly and still feels like a fraud.
people.friend_view: His best friend Terrence says Andre is a born leader and a performer who needs to be the guy with the answers. He never admits he is struggling. Something has been off lately: he's jumpy about money and about his phone.
people.self_view: A servant pouring himself out for young people; humble, just a vessel. He thinks the betting is a small thing he will stop after the wedding.
people.faith: Evangelical, raised Southern Baptist, earnest and firm. He preaches grace well and finds it far easier to hand to others than to take for himself.
people.weighing: Whether to tell Brianna before the wedding. The debt keeps growing. A boy in his youth group has just confided a gambling problem to him, and Andre doesn't know what to say.

people.name: Ioana Popescu
people.situation: Turin, Italy, from a village near Suceava, Romania. Live-in carer for Signor Bertolino, an 88-year-old widower with Parkinson's; six days a week, round the clock. Her daughter Daria (9) lives with Ioana's mother in Romania. Divorced; her ex pays nothing. Saving to build a house back home.
people.temperament: Ioana's patience was built, not given. She lifts Signor Bertolino out of bed, shaves him, cuts his food, and listens to the same war stories every afternoon, nodding as if they were new. He is grumpy and sometimes says hurtful things; she answers mildly and then scrubs the kitchen very hard. Her Italian is good now, but she keeps her words few. On her one free afternoon she meets other Romanian women at a cafe near the station and becomes, for three hours, loud and funny and bossy. She video-calls Daria every evening, and it is the best and worst part of the day. She saves almost everything: she buys the cheapest bread, never goes to the cinema, has worn the same winter coat for six years, and sends money home for bricks and windows. She resents her ex, her brother who never helps their mother, and sometimes the old man, and she is ashamed of the resentment. When the family asks her to do more, she never says no; she simply takes it on. She is slow to trust Italians and slower to trust men. She keeps a small icon of the Mother of God on the chest of drawers and kisses it before she sleeps.
people.friend_view: Her friend Mihaela says Ioana lets everyone use her: the Italian family, the ex, her own brother. She swallows everything, and one day she will explode or fall ill. She is the hardest-working person alive.
people.self_view: A mother doing what she must so her daughter has a future. Not a victim, just practical. She thinks she is more bitter than she really is.
people.faith: Romanian Orthodox. Goes to the Romanian parish in Turin when she can find cover, keeps the fasts loosely, says the evening prayers. Her faith is a lifeline and a piece of home.
people.weighing: Daria cried on the phone and begged her to come home. The house needs two more years of wages. Signor Bertolino's son wants her to stay on after his father dies to look after an aunt.

people.name: Jennifer "Jenn" Tremblay
people.situation: Laval, near Montreal, Quebec, Canada. Dental hygienist. Married to Marc, an electrician; two children aged 14 and 11, in hockey and dance. Mortgage, car payments and a camping trailer. Healthy apart from some poor sleep.
people.temperament: Jenn is a pretty ordinary, good-natured person. She chats easily with patients about their kids and their holidays, switching between French and English without noticing. At home she is the organiser: the calendar on the fridge, the carpool group chat, the hockey tournament in Sherbrooke. Some weeks she is cheerful and patient; other weeks she is short with everyone and knows it's because she's tired. She gets mad and gets over it. She is neither cheap nor extravagant: she clips grocery coupons and then books a week in Cuba in February. She talks a fair amount with friends and listens reasonably well. She likes a glass of wine on Friday and a true-crime podcast while folding laundry. She can be a pushover with her kids about screens and then cracks down all at once. She starts projects around the house and finishes most of them, eventually. She is sentimental about her grandmother, who was very devout, and keeps her rosary in a drawer without using it. She worries a normal amount, mostly about her son and his phone, and about her mother's heart. She forgets birthdays, remembers them late, and sends a nice card with an apology.
people.friend_view: Her best friend Isabelle says Jenn is the glue of the hockey-parent group: fun, steady, a bit soft with her kids, a good friend who is always slightly overbooked.
people.self_view: An ordinary busy mom. Not religious, not unhappy, just busy. She would like more time for herself.
people.faith: Baptised and confirmed Catholic, like most people she grew up with. Hasn't been to Mass except for funerals and her grandmother's anniversary Mass. Unsure; thinks there is "something" and sometimes wishes her children had what her grandmother had.
people.weighing: Her mother's upcoming heart surgery. Her daughter recently asked why they never go to church. Marc wants a bigger trailer and she is not sure they can afford it.

people.name: Nadia Haddad
people.situation: Beirut, Lebanon (Achrafieh). Pharmacist who owns a small neighbourhood pharmacy. Lost most of her savings in the 2019 banking collapse. Her husband Georges works in Dubai and comes home three times a year; two children aged 16 and 12. Supports her elderly father. Chronic migraines.
people.temperament: Nadia talks fast and worries faster. Behind the counter she explains doses, scolds old men about their blood pressure, slips free samples to women who can't pay, and asks after everyone's children. Her phone buzzes all day: suppliers, her father, the school group chat, Georges. She is funny, often darkly so; her jokes about power cuts and the banks make customers laugh at things that are not funny. Inside, she runs disaster scenarios all night: another explosion, an insulin shortage, her son getting into trouble, her husband meeting someone in Dubai. She checks the news fifteen times a day. When she is frightened she gets bossy and controlling and starts rearranging shelves and recounting stock. She lets her father criticise her endlessly without answering back, then snaps at her daughter an hour later. She is generous, sometimes recklessly: she keeps a shelf of medicines on credit for families who may never pay. She sleeps badly, and the migraines come when she finally stops, usually on the first day of a holiday. When she prays she mostly bargains. Her laugh is louder than she means it to be, and people across the street turn round.
people.friend_view: Her friend Rita says Nadia carries the whole street on her back and would rather die than admit she is exhausted. She worries herself sick and then makes everyone laugh so they won't notice.
people.self_view: A survivor who laughs at everything. She thinks she is calm in a crisis, and in the moment she is; she doesn't count the sleepless nights.
people.faith: Maronite Catholic. Sunday Mass at her parish, a strong devotion to St. Charbel, and more than one pilgrimage to his monastery at Annaya. Her faith is anxious and heartfelt.
people.weighing: Georges wants the family to join him in Dubai. Her father won't leave Lebanon and she won't leave him. Her son wants to study abroad.

people.name: Kwame Asante
people.situation: Kumasi, Ghana. Retired headmaster of a Presbyterian secondary school. Widowed, then remarried five years ago to Akosua (58). Four grown children, eleven grandchildren. Church elder. Comfortable pension plus rent from rooms. Good health apart from mild prostate trouble.
people.temperament: Kwame likes to be listened to, and usually he is. He wears a pressed shirt every day, reads the newspaper front to back, and has an opinion on each page. At family gatherings he gives a short speech that is never short. He quizzes his grandchildren on times tables and capital cities and is delighted when they get them right. His generosity is public: he has paid school fees for a dozen children who aren't his, and he would like that known, gently. He is stubborn about how things should be done: church matters, his late wife's grave, the leaking roof he refuses to have replaced. He rarely admits a mistake; when he is wrong, he changes the subject with a proverb. He was patient with thousands of pupils and is impatient with his eldest son, whom he still corrects in front of others. He rises at five, prays, walks, and naps at two. He laughs heartily at his own jokes. With Akosua he is courteous and a little formal, as if she were a visiting inspector he respects. He is deeply proud of his life and grateful for it, and he sleeps well.
people.friend_view: His younger brother says Kwame is a good man who has been a headmaster for fifty years and has forgotten how to be anything else. His own son has never once heard him say "I'm sorry." If you asked, he would admit he is proud, laughing.
people.self_view: A fair and principled man who has served his community and his church; strict but loving. He would say he watches his pride carefully, and thinks he does it well.
people.faith: Presbyterian Church of Ghana. Elder for thirty years, leads morning devotions, reads the Twi Bible. His faith is confident, orderly and proud of its history.
people.weighing: His eldest son (46) lost his job and asked for a loan. Kwame wants to give it, and also wants to give a lecture with it. The church session is arguing over a new building, and he is against it.

people.name: Pieter van den Berg
people.situation: Utrecht, Netherlands. Team lead for IT support at a hospital. Married to Marieke, a primary school teacher; two teenagers aged 17 and 14. Owns a terraced house and cycles to work. His father recently moved into a care home.
people.temperament: Pieter is a pleasant, middle-of-the-road man. He cycles to work in any weather, drinks too much coffee, and fixes the same printer every week without much fuss. He is direct in the Dutch way: he says what he thinks in meetings and doesn't mind being disagreed with. At weekends he cooks, not very well, with great confidence. He has moods. He is grumpy when the train is cancelled or the kids leave their bikes blocking the gate, and cheerful when Ajax wins. He is fairly generous: buys a round, gives to the Red Cross, but checks the price of cheese. He likes people in moderation; a birthday party is fine, but by ten he is glancing at the clock. He is no early adopter. He took two years to change phones and a year to choose a new kitchen, but once the kitchen was ordered it was done on schedule. He visits his father at the care home twice a week, finds it sad and dull, and goes anyway. He worries a bit about his daughter's exams and a little about his own blood pressure. He is neither especially anxious nor especially calm. On holiday he reads one thriller and finishes it.
people.friend_view: Marieke says Pieter is reliable, good company and a bit stubborn about small things like how to load the dishwasher. Nothing hidden: what you see is what you get.
people.self_view: An average bloke, content and practical. He more or less agrees with Marieke.
people.faith: Member of the Protestant Church in the Netherlands. Goes perhaps once a month and at Christmas, and joins the choir for the Good Friday music. Believes in a general way, with doubts he doesn't lose sleep over.
people.weighing: Whether his father is getting good enough care and whether to push the home about it. His son wants to take a gap year. His doctor wants him to lose seven kilos.

people.name: Nomvula Dlamini
people.situation: Soweto, South Africa. Administrative officer in a Johannesburg municipal department. Married to Sipho, who owns and drives a minibus taxi; two children aged 12 and 7. Also raising her late sister's son (15). Owns a house in Orlando East. Money is fine but stretched by extended family. High blood pressure.
people.temperament: Nomvula gets up at 4:45, irons the school uniforms, and catches a lift to the office by seven. At work she is pleasant, neither the loudest nor the quietest. She chats in the tea room, does her job properly, and is irritated by colleagues who drift in late, though she only says so to her friend Lindiwe. At home she is warm and firm, and the children know where the line is. Some evenings she is patient; some evenings she snaps, and then makes vetkoek to make up for it. She gives money to family when asked, sometimes more than she should, and balances it by skipping her own hair appointment. She enjoys a party, the catch-up after a funeral, the savings club's year-end braai, and she also enjoys a Sunday afternoon nap with the TV on. She can be a little stubborn with Sipho over money; they argue and then laugh about it. She worries about her nephew, who went quiet after his mother died, but she worries in a practical way and asks the school counsellor to check on him. She starts things and finishes most of them. She is neither very anxious nor very carefree. She belts out hymns in the car.
people.friend_view: Lindiwe says Nomvula is steady and sensible, maybe too soft with relatives who ask for money, and the person you want beside you in a crisis.
people.self_view: An ordinary working mother. Blessed, tired, doing fine.
people.faith: Methodist Church of Southern Africa. Wears the red and white of the women's prayer union on Thursdays when she can, and goes to Sunday worship most weeks. Her faith is communal and sung.
people.weighing: Her nephew's marks have dropped and he won't talk about it. Her brother wants to borrow money for his bride price. Her blood-pressure pills make her dizzy.

hard_items.why: Both sides are self-regard she would not own: she waves thanks away (so not A) and sees herself as simple (so not B), though she is privately bossy about how things should be done.
Both are true of her: money keeps her awake, and she keeps a quiet list of people who never thanked her. Her self-view denies the second, so she picks money, but it was close.
Answering as a mother she would say the family, but strangers and the parish get her sunniest side while her son gets complaints behind his back. Either answer feels like a confession, so 0.
She does not think of her life as having 'projects'; neither option describes how a retired sari-sari store owner sees herself.
She sees herself regretting neither. Dropping a plan because of doubt is not her, and 'not listening to advice' is something she would not admit.
Neither fits. She is not someone who gives up under correction, and she would never say she lets details slip. She only knows she prefers correction to be gentle.
Neither side is him. Criticism makes him angry rather than sinking him, and praise does not linger either. The item has no 'it makes me defensive' option, so the lean is arbitrary.

When he is low he reaches for cans and goes silent for days. 'Things I shouldn't want' could mean the drink or could read as sexual, so he does not know which he is admitting to. He would pick 'heavy' to avoid it.
Both daydreams feel awkward for a 34-year-old bloke to admit (a private one, or wanting to impress). His real daydreams are about telling his ex's solicitor where to go, and neither side covers that.
'Told I can do better' is what makes him bristle, not try harder, but 'told I did well' does not really motivate him either. The item assumes one of them works.
He knows, since Ellie's question, that the lads at work get the fun version and home gets the shouting, but his self-view as a good dad resists saying it. His answer is a reluctant -1.

He says something at work when a calculation is wrong, but he never feels 'the heat rise', and he does not 'give people room' either, because he rechecks everything. The anger wording and the action are fused on side A.
His real response to an argument is to leave the room. 'Calm things down' is the nearer option but still wrong; neither side lets him withdraw.
On a slow afternoon he is in the allotment or reading. He neither snacks nor drifts wishing he were elsewhere, so both sides are wrong.
Nothing much pulls at him when he is worn out, perhaps a beer. The 'look or thought that lingers' side is one a reserved Catholic man would never pick on a quiz, whatever the truth.
Both are genuinely hard for him: parting with saved money and admitting someone else's way was better. His self-view ('I am open to other views') stops him choosing B, so he lands at 0.
Neither criticism nor praise moves him for days. He would shrug at both sides.
He does not think of himself as a daydreamer. A private daydream is unadmittable, and wanting to impress people is not how he sees himself, though being proven right on the numbers comes close.
He regrets neither: he seldom drops plans and does not believe he ignores good advice. The item assumes one of these is a regret.
'I let things slip if nobody checks' is the opposite of him (he is the checker), and 'too much correction and I give up' is not him either. He leaned to details only because he values them.
Her real pattern is rushing in, but she sees her problem as too little time, so she'd say her regrets are things she never got round to. The item pulls her self-view against her actual habit.
Neither pull fits her. When she's worn out she gets up and cleans or does one more task. Food or a lingering look is a guess.
She doesn't treat herself and she doesn't hold back to stay hard. She just keeps working, so both sides miss her.
She rarely drops plans because someone doubts them, and she doesn't see herself ignoring good advice. Her projects die of boredom, which the item doesn't offer.
Both halves are true of her. She bristles at correction, and she lets details slip once the novelty wears off.
She's a 74-year-old widow and every day runs on the same routine, so 'a weekend with nothing planned' means little to her. 'Like a gift' is too cheerful for her, and she isn't restless either.
She has no unfinished projects of either kind, so the item doesn't apply to her.
Both sides are wrong for her. Correction makes her angry rather than making her give up, and she never lets details slip.
Criticism doesn't sink her, it makes her angry. Praise doesn't lift her, she distrusts it. Neither side fits.
She does snap, but she'd never admit to wishing she hadn't. She calls it honesty, so the B side carries a regret she won't own.
Both are true. She doesn't notice when she wounds Maria, and she holds every slight, down to who missed a memorial.
Both are true. She hides her loneliness and her anger at God, and she also says cutting things at the wrong moment.
Neither food nor a lingering look is what pulls at her when she's tired. She sits in the dark with her prayer rope.
She neither drops plans because of doubters nor ignores advice she thinks is good. She rejects the advice outright, so neither regret fits.
He sees himself as chill and sure it'll work out, but underneath he worries about everything ahead. His self-view and his real anxiety pull opposite ways.
He never really has 'nothing to do', because games and short videos fill every gap. So he can't say whether his thoughts settle or get worse, and 'better off busy' doesn't describe him.
Both are true. Too much correction and he quits, and he also lets things slip when nobody checks.
He starts things easily and drops them around day nine. That's the middle, not the first step or the last ten percent. Only the big choice, his major, is a first-step problem.
'Even when I have plenty' doesn't fit someone with $4,000 of loans and a part-time wage. He worries about money because he really doesn't have enough, which the item doesn't allow for.
He'd say yes to a friend to avoid awkwardness, but he's broke and anxious about money. So neither giving on impulse nor keeping some back describes him cleanly.
Neither side fits her: she does not stop the home temper and she does not say sorry a lot either; she picked A only because she does not see herself as someone who apologises and repeats.
Both options describe a weakness she would not own: she neither gives up under correction nor lets details slip; she simply dislikes being second-guessed, which is not offered.
When things go badly she gets short and bossy, not sad and not restless; both options miss the irritability that is her real pattern.
Genuinely both: she hides tiredness and weakness from everyone but speaks bluntly to juniors and her husband, so she had to sit at 0.
She half-knows her patients get the best of her and it bothers her at night, but her self-view says she is fair to everyone; answering it honestly as herself was uncomfortable.
She rarely drops plans for anyone's doubts and does not believe she ignores good advice, so neither regret feels like hers.
Neither side is him: he does not give up under correction and he does not let things slip; he checks everything himself, so B was picked only because it names details.
After a bad day he goes cold and withdrawn, which is neither plainly angry nor plainly low.
Piled-up work does not make him feel buried or come alive; he just grinds through it late at night, and the anxious option only half fits.
Words come easily at work and in precise cold anger, but hard at home about feelings; the item does not say which setting.
He rarely gets loud, so he sees himself as slow to anger, yet the sudden sternness over a maths score says otherwise; the item assumes anger is visible.
Both eat at her, but she avoids thinking about money (statements in a drawer, afraid of the bank app), so she would honestly name people even though money is the bigger weight.
Her daydreams are about rescue or romance (the man messaging her) as much as being admired; she would not admit the first, so the answer leans to the flattering side.
She sees herself as a determined fighter but restarts diets every Monday and trusts people too fast; her self-view and her pattern point opposite ways.
Her anger flares and fades quickly, but she stews for a day over what she said; the item blurs anger lasting with regret lasting.
She keeps smiling in public and cries alone on the back step, so the sadness does not show; restless scrolling and shopping is closer but not quite 'wanting to be anywhere else'.
A 78-year-old who 'doesn't think too hard' would say he doesn't daydream about either; both a secret daydream and wanting to impress feel foreign to him.
What eats at him is June's decline, which is neither money nor what people did to him; money only wins because memory care costs something.
Both sides are wrong for him: he doesn't give up under correction and a machinist doesn't let details slip.
He hides the sadness and isn't restless to be elsewhere; going out to bang around in the garage is the closest match, but it's a loose fit.
He doesn't replay arguments, and his self-view is that he can take it straight, but he knows he's stubborn; he'd grudgingly pick B without really recognising himself.
He'd say he finishes what he starts; a garage project put down since June's diagnosis is the only thing that fits.
He wouldn't see himself as needing either; the push he needs (doctor, aide) is something he'd deny from his own view.
Both are true of her: her sharp remarks land without her noticing, and one raised eyebrow can also sting her all day.
Both again: she guards everything about herself but blurts opinions at the wrong moment. The item treats those as opposites when for her they sit side by side.
She thinks out loud at dinner and argues out loud online, then lies awake replaying it all in her head.
'I feel things heavily' clashes with her self-image as unsentimental, but 'light' is plainly false for a pessimist; she picks serious for grim realism, not for feeling.
Her self-view says she doesn't care what people think, but she's easily hurt and lies awake replaying; the honest answer and the self-image pull in opposite directions.
Neither daydream really fits; winning the argument in front of people is the nearest.
She enjoys performing at dinner parties but isn't ambitious; neither 'fear' nor 'chance to shine' is what really moves her.

A devout young man who keeps the fasts would be ashamed to admit to the 'look that lingers' side, so food becomes the safe answer whatever the truth is; the item may just measure which vice feels admissible.
Same problem: a daydream 'you'd rather nobody knew about' (for example the woman at church) is something he wouldn't confess, so he picks being a provider his family is proud of.
'The people at home' is ambiguous for an immigrant: his roommates (who get his irritation) or his mother and sisters in Addis (who get his laughter).
Neither side fits: he doesn't give up under correction and doesn't let details slip.
Neither pattern is his; he's polite but reserved, and neither 'rarely sorry' nor 'sorry a lot' describes him.
He doesn't argue, so there's nothing to replay; he's stubborn but wouldn't call it trouble taking correction. He picked A only because the roommate irritations stay with him.
He's sad but it doesn't show, and 'restless' is only half-right (he leaves for his cousin's when it piles up).
Neither is hard for her: she lets housemates eat her food and admits others are better all the time, so she had to pick the 'less easy' side.
Both sides are wrong: she never judges others for overindulging, but she also thinks twice about everything, including a meal.
Side B says 'even when I have plenty'; she has no savings and a student loan, so the worry is real, not a quirk, and the option does not fit.
Both work on a people-pleaser: being asked for help means she never says no, and being told plainly spares her deciding.
'A daydream you'd rather nobody knew about' is vague; her secret is reading Luke at night, which is not a daydream, and wanting to be liked is not quite 'impressed with you'.
An empty weekend feels like a gift to someone this tired, yet idle time is exactly when she spirals; the two items pull against each other.
She gives her best to everyone, customers, patients, housemates and both parents; 'people at home' is ambiguous for someone in a share house who is also the family go-between.
